rule: A local tax is applied only when the user selects that place. New York City tax is never applied to the rest of New York. A custom percent replaces the selected place and is applied to gross wages. Local rates change during the year; each entry shows the date it was last checked.

jurisdictions.name: New York City
jurisdictions.residentOnlyNote: New York City income tax applies to residents of the five boroughs. Working in Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, or Staten Island does not, by itself, create a city income tax.

source.name: New York State, New York City tax rates

jurisdictions.notes: New York City residents pay city income tax at 3.078%, 3.762%, 3.819% and 3.876% of New York taxable income. It follows where you live: working in the five boroughs does not create city tax. The city's household and school tax credits are not included, so a real return can be a little lower.

jurisdictions.sourceLabel: Yonkers resident surcharge / nonresident earnings tax

source.name: New York State, Yonkers tax

jurisdictions.notes: Yonkers residents pay a surcharge of 16.75% of their New York State income tax. People who work in Yonkers and live elsewhere pay 0.5% of the wages earned there.

jurisdictions.name: Philadelphia

source.name: City of Philadelphia, Wage Tax (employers)

jurisdictions.notes: Rates effective July 1, 2026: 3.735% for residents and 3.425% for nonresidents who work in the city (3.74% and 3.43% from July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026). The estimate applies the current rate to the whole year. The wage tax is charged on gross compensation; 401(k) contributions do not reduce it.

jurisdictions.name: Pittsburgh

source.name: City of Pittsburgh, Earned Income Tax

jurisdictions.notes: Pittsburgh residents pay a 3% earned income tax (1% to the city and 2% to Pittsburgh Public Schools). People who work in the city and live elsewhere in Pennsylvania pay their home municipality's rate or 1%, whichever is higher; the work-only switch uses 1%. The tax follows Pennsylvania's definition of wages, so 401(k) contributions stay in and health premiums come out. Everyone who works in the city and earns $12,000 or more also pays the $52 Local Services Tax, shown as its own line.

jurisdictions.name: Detroit

source.name: Michigan Department of Treasury, City of Detroit income tax withholding guide (Form 5469), 2026

jurisdictions.notes: Detroit taxes residents at 2.4% and nonresidents who work in the city at 1.2%. The tax starts from the same wages as the federal return, so 401(k) and cafeteria-plan amounts come out, and each person on the return gets a $600 exemption. A nonresident who works part of the time outside Detroit owes tax only on the Detroit share; this estimate assumes all of the work is in the city.

jurisdictions.name: Columbus, Ohio

source.name: City of Columbus income tax division

jurisdictions.notes: Columbus's municipal income tax is 2.5% of qualifying wages, for residents and for people who work there. Qualifying wages follow Medicare wages: 401(k) contributions stay in, and cafeteria-plan health premiums, FSA and HSA amounts come out. If you live in one Ohio city and work in another, the city where you live usually gives a credit for tax paid to the other. This estimate applies only the city you select.

jurisdictions.notes: A Portland resident inside both Metro and Multnomah County can owe two extra income taxes on Oregon taxable income: Metro's 1% supportive housing services tax above $128,000 ($205,000 joint) for 2026, and Multnomah County's Preschool for All tax of 1.5% above $125,000 ($200,000 joint) plus another 1.5% above $250,000 ($400,000 joint). Contributions to retirement plans and cafeteria plans are not taxed. The separate 0.5% payroll expense tax is paid by employers and is not a paycheck line.

jurisdictions.name: Denver
jurisdictions.sourceLabel: Denver occupational privilege tax · $5.75 a month

source.name: City and County of Denver, Tax Guide Topic 61: Occupational Privilege Taxes

jurisdictions.notes: Denver charges employees who work in the city and earn at least $500 in a month an occupational privilege tax of $5.75 a month ($69 a year). It is a flat amount, not a percent of pay, and it is owed by where you work, not where you live.
